summary: Specifies a procedure that uses several Path Computation Elements to compute shortest constrained traffic engineering paths across multiple domains. Computation proceeds backward from the destination domain toward the source. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: To plan a trip through several countries, you ask the last country for routes in, then pass the best options back one country at a time until you reach home.

subtitle: How a chain of path computation servers finds the shortest constrained path across several network domains without revealing their insides.

tldr.problem: Finding the shortest constrained traffic engineering path across several domains (IGP areas or Autonomous Systems) is hard when no topology information may be shared between the domains.
tldr.mechanism: The request is passed from one Path Computation Element (PCE) to the next until the destination domain is reached. Then each PCE in turn builds a Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT) from its own view plus the tree it received, and passes it back toward the source.
tldr.outcome: For a given sequence of domains, the procedure finds the optimal (shortest) constrained path while keeping each domain's topology confidential. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5441 is a Proposed Standard from April 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PCEP messages of RFC 5440.

sections.title: Why Per-Domain Computation Falls Short
sections.content:
Large networks are split into domains: IGP areas or Autonomous Systems. Requirements for inter-area and inter-AS MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) are stated in RFC 4105 and RFC 4216, and the framework is in RFC 4726.

RFC 5152 computes the path domain by domain during signaling, at the entry boundary node of each domain. That meets some of the requirements but cannot guarantee an optimal (shortest) inter-domain constrained path, and it cannot efficiently compute a set of diversely routed inter-domain TE LSPs.

This RFC uses the PCE architecture of RFC 4655 instead. Here "optimal" means the shortest path satisfying the constraints that would be found if the network were one flat IGP network between source and destination. That needs consistent metrics in every domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If each country plans only its own piece of the trip, the whole trip may not be the shortest. BRPC lets the countries cooperate so the full trip is the shortest one.

sections.title: Assumptions and Terms
sections.content:
The procedure assumes each domain is TE enabled and that no topology or resource information is distributed between domains. This is mandated by RFC 4105 and RFC 4216 and is critical for IGP/BGP scalability and confidentiality. Constraints such as affinity or color may be translated at domain boundaries through local policy mappings.

The sequence of domains (the domain path) is either administratively predetermined or discovered by means outside this document. The PCC MAY give the sequence using the Include Route Object (IRO) from RFC 5440.

A boundary node (BN) is an ABR for inter-area TE or an ASBR for inter-AS TE. The entry BN of domain(n) connects domain(n-1) to domain(n), and the exit BN connects domain(n) to domain(n+1). PCE(i) is the PCE with the scope of domain(i).
sections.plainLanguage: Each country keeps its map private, so only the border gates are known to the others. The route through the countries is already chosen before planning starts.

sections.title: The Backward-Recursive Procedure
sections.content:
The PCC sends a PCReq to a PCE in its domain. The request is forwarded between PCEs, domain by domain, until the PCE of the destination domain is reached. That PCE creates a tree of potential paths to the destination, the Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT), and returns it in a PCRep to the previous PCE. Each PCE in turn adds to the VSPT and passes it back.

In detail: PCE(n) computes VSPT(n), the shortest constrained paths between every entry BN of domain(n) and the destination, using an algorithm such as CSPF. For i = n-1 down to 2, PCE(i) computes VSPT(i) from its own TED and the information in VSPT(i+1). For inter-AS computation it also adds the inter-AS TE links. Finally PCE(1) computes the end-to-end shortest constrained path and returns it to the PCC in a PCRep.

Each branch of a VSPT may be an explicit path or a loose path listing only the BN, which preserves confidentiality; path keys can then be used to retrieve explicit paths per domain during signaling. A PCE that can compute for several consecutive domains SHOULD do so before passing the PCRep back. With Equal Cost Multi-Path, more than one path could be returned. The procedure makes no assumption about the path computation algorithm or whether the LSP is contiguous, nested or stitched.
sections.plainLanguage: The question travels forward to the last country. Then the answers travel backward, and each country adds its own part, so the first country can pick the best full route.

sections.title: PCEP Extensions
sections.content:
BRPC defines one new flag in the RP object of the PCReq message: the VSPT flag, bit number 25. When set, it tells PCEs that the PCC requests an inter-domain TE LSP computation using BRPC, that is, the shortest constrained paths from the destination to the set of entry boundary nodes.

Because path segments from a downstream PCE MUST come with their costs, the C flag of the METRIC object in the PCReq MUST be set. Setting the O bit of the RP object is the requester's choice.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small checkbox on the request that says "please use the cooperating-countries method, and tell me the cost of each piece."

sections.title: How a VSPT Is Encoded
sections.content:
A VSPT travels inside a PCRep message as a non-ordered list of Explicit Route Objects (EROs). Each ERO is a path segment from one boundary node to the destination named in the END-POINT object of the PCReq.

The RFC's example has three ABRs between area 0 and area 2, with destination D. The VSPT computed by the PCE serving area 2 is ERO1 (ABR1 to A to B to D), ERO2 (ABR2 to D) and ERO3 (ABR3 to C to D). The PCReq, PCRep, END-POINT and ERO are defined in RFC 5440.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a list of little routes, one from each border gate to the destination, in no special order.

sections.title: Failures and Error Reporting
sections.content:
If a PCE on the domain path does not recognize the VSPT flag, it sends a PCErr to the upstream PCE with Error-Type 4 (Not supported object) and Error-value 4 (Unsupported parameter), as RFC 5440 states, and the request is cancelled without further notification. If a PCE recognizes the procedure but does not support it, it MUST return a PCErr with the new Error-Type 13, "BRPC procedure completion failure", Error-value 1. The PCErr MUST be relayed to the requesting PCC.

If a PCE must relay a request to a downstream PCE and none is available, it MUST send a negative reply containing a NO-PATH object. That object MUST carry a NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV with the new bit "BRPC path computation chain unavailable" set.
sections.plainLanguage: If one country does not know the method, or the next country is not answering, the traveler is told clearly so the trip is not left hanging.

sections.title: Diversity, Reoptimization and Metrics
sections.content:
A PCC can ask for a set of diverse TE LSPs by setting the L, N or S flag of the SVEC object (link, node or SRLG diversity). Each PCE along the chain MUST honor this during VSPT computation. Since a PCE computes the path segments of the VSPT together, BRPC can find diverse paths under objective functions such as minimizing the sum of the costs. A two-step approach (compute one path, remove its elements, compute another) cannot guarantee that a solution is found even if one exists, and needs two serialized TE LSP setups.

For optimality, BRPC guarantees the shortest constrained path will be found, subject to policy. After a network change in a domain, guaranteeing optimality requires re-executing the whole procedure. For reoptimization, the path in use is supplied in the request so PCEs can avoid double bandwidth accounting.

For inter-AS TE, metric normalization between ASes may be required. One option is for providers to agree on a TE metric normalization scheme and ask for the TE metric in the METRIC object. Combining BRPC with per-domain computation (RFC 5152) means end-to-end optimality can no longer be guaranteed.
sections.plainLanguage: Planning two separate routes at once works better than planning one, then trying to squeeze in a second. And if the countries count distance in different units, they must agree on one first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BRPC relies on PCEP and so is subject to the attacks listed in Section 10 of RFC 5440: spoofing, snooping, falsification and denial of service. An implementation MAY also support a policy module controlling when a PCE participates in BRPC, for example by origin of requests or number of requests per second.

The procedure does not increase the information exchanged between ASes and preserves topology confidentiality, in line with RFC 4105 and RFC 4216.
sections.plainLanguage: The same safety rules as the basic path-computation protocol apply, and the method does not make countries share any more secrets than before.
